title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
The page continues the 'Dilucidationes' that Euler attaches to E420, where he re-explains his new method of variations for functions of one variable. In §32 the abstract problem from §31 is put geometrically. Take a curve AM over the axis AP, with abscissa x = AP and ordinate y = PM, and let W = ∫Z dx be the value of the functional along it. Now take any other curve αμ that differs infinitely little from AM and compute the same integral along it. The difference between the two values is exactly the variation δW that the formal calculus of §§1–30 produces. In modern terms, δW is the first-order part of J[y+εη] − J[y].

§33 gives the standard example, the descent time along a curve. AP = x is taken as the vertical axis, measured downward from the starting point A. A body starting from rest at A has speed at M proportional to √x (Galileo/Torricelli, v = √(2gx), constant dropped). The arc element is ds = dx√(1+p²) with dy = p dx. So the time over the element Mm is dx√(1+p²)/√x, and the descent time is T = ∫dx√(1+p²)/√x, i.e. Z = √(1+p²)/√x. The variation is then the difference between the descent times along the nearby curve αμ (from α to μ) and along AM. This is the brachistochrone functional, written with x as the vertical variable.

§34 begins the question of how the integral is to be fixed. In this example it must be taken so that it vanishes at x = 0, the starting point A. The next page generalises this: a fixed lower limit, either x = 0 or some given x. The surrounding text serves to justify the formal δ-calculus by a direct comparison of curves. The following page adds that the comparison curves need only be unbroken (no corners or jumps) and may even be 'discontinuous' in Euler's sense, i.e. drawn freely by hand.
errors: No mathematical errors. The constant factor (√(2g)) is omitted, which is harmless since only proportionality matters. The integrand is singular at x = 0 (1/√x), but the integral is convergent; Euler does not comment on this, which is a routine omission.

ideas.what: Interpretation of the variation δW as the difference between the values of ∫Z dx on a given curve and on an infinitely near comparison curve
ideas.modern_name: First variation / Gateaux derivative of a functional
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1755/1760–62) for the δ-algorithm; Euler (E296, E297, 1764/66; E420) for this interpretation
ideas.where_published: E296/E297 (Elementa calculi variationum; Analytica explicatio); E420 §§31–36; later Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E385)

ideas.what: Descent time along a curve as the integral ∫dx√(1+p²)/√x, with x taken as the vertical
ideas.usually_credited_to: Johann Bernoulli (1696/97); variational formulation Euler (Methodus inveniendi, E65, 1744)
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (1744); Mechanica (E15/E16)

ideas.what: Fixing the lower limit of integration so that the integral vanishes at the starting point (x = 0 or a given x)
ideas.modern_name: Fixed-endpoint integral functional / definite integral over [a,x]

deep.surprise_reason: This is a pedagogical restatement of the variation as a functional difference, illustrated with the classical brachistochrone integral. Both are well documented in Euler's own works and in standard histories of the calculus of variations (Goldstine, Fraser). The only mildly interesting remark, that comparison curves may be freely drawn, is on the next page and is also known in the literature.
transcription_corrections: The transcription of this page matches the image essentially exactly: 'cuiuspiam' (with a hyphenated break on the previous page), 'ſit = W' and 'Mm' are all as printed.
